title: Cambridge Aerospace raises $300M Series C at $3.4B on AI-guided cheap-interceptor thesis
subtitle: Two-year-old UK defense startup led by MIT's Steven Barrett takes on Russia's drone tempo with a Skyhammer interceptor priced for attrition warfare — DFJ Growth leads, valuation eight times its 2025 Series A.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Cambridge Aerospace closed a $300 million Series C on August 10 at a $3.4 billion valuation, led by DFJ Growth with Lux Capital, Accel, Lakestar, Never Lift, Ora Global and Elad Gil. Founded in September 2024 by MIT's Steven Barrett, the UK startup has now raised more than $630 million total and jumped from a $400M Series A valuation in summer 2025 to $3.4B in roughly a year. Lead product Skyhammer is a rocket-powered interceptor with 30+ km range and 700 km/h top speed, designed as the cheap layer in a stacked anti-drone and cruise-missile defense.

The AI story here is not a chatbot — it is autonomous targeting at unit costs low enough to burn through Shahed-class drones without depleting a magazine of million-dollar Patriots. Modern strike campaigns fire drones at a rate that inverts the economics of legacy air defense; if an interceptor costs 20x its target, the defender loses on price even when it wins on tempo. Cambridge is betting that computer-vision guidance, autonomy for terminal engagement, and manufacturable rocket motors can bring a per-shot cost to something like a car, not a house.

The round mirrors what Anduril, Helsing and Shield AI have been signaling for two years: defense-tech capital has decoupled from consumer software cycles, and the buyers — the UK MoD, the Pentagon, several European militaries — are ordering in volume rather than pilots. Cambridge already holds UK government contracts and is building a Skyhammer factory. The DFJ Growth-led round joins fresh capital from Elad Gil and Spark Capital's earlier Series B; the investor list looks like a Silicon Valley bet on Europe's rearmament being real.

For learners: the frontier for applied AI is no longer only chatbots and coding assistants. Autonomy, sensor fusion, and real-time control are becoming the interesting problems again, and defense is one of the few sectors where the physics constraint and the cost constraint both bite. If you are early-career and looking at where AI engineering skill compounds, watch the companies where a model has to close a loop in the physical world under time pressure — that is where the hardest engineering, and the most durable careers, are building right now.
